title: Communication with pressured speech
stem: A client with mania speaks rapidly and changes topics when the nurse asks, "Tell me about your sleep over the past week." What approach best helps obtain this information?
options: Ask one brief sleep question and gently redirect to it
Invite an uninterrupted account of the whole previous day
Provide a full written history form to complete
Repeat the original open-ended question at the same length
why: A concrete limited question with calm redirection matches the current attention difficulty.
A broad narrative may increase topic shifts before obtaining the needed detail.
A full form adds processing demands and may not fit current distractibility.
Repeating the same broad demand does not adapt to the observed difficulty.
takeaway: Keep communication concrete and focused during manic distractibility.
learningObjective: Keep communication concrete and focused during manic distractibility.

title: Feeling well and treatment continuation
stem: A client with bipolar disorder feels well and wants to stop follow-up, saying, "I thought appointments were for when I am ill." Which response best supports an informed decision?
options: You could return when the early warning signs begin again.
Follow-up also supports staying well; what concerns do you have about continuing?
We can focus future visits on whether you need another prescription.
We can schedule visits farther apart while you feel well.
why: Symptom-triggered contact is useful but does not explain preventive review during stability.
Explaining the maintenance purpose while exploring concerns supports a shared review rather than automatic cessation.
Prescription access is one function, but narrowing visits to refills misses broader maintenance needs.
Spacing may be considered collaboratively, but does not first clarify the client's misunderstanding about the purpose of follow-up during wellness.
takeaway: Explain the purpose of maintenance care during bipolar stability.
learningObjective: Explain the purpose of maintenance care during bipolar stability.

title: New reduced alertness during routine care
stem: A client with schizophrenia usually needs prompts to begin hygiene but then performs it safely. Today the nurse also notices new drowsiness, slower walking and difficulty staying awake after a medicine change. What should happen next?
options: Increase the frequency of the usual hygiene prompts
Complete hygiene earlier before the client lies down
Continue the familiar routine and compare it tomorrow
Assess the new alertness change and seek a medication review
why: More prompts do not evaluate the new sedation and slowed movement.
Timing changes may support a stable routine but do not explain a new post-change presentation.
Waiting may miss a clinically significant treatment effect or another cause.
The new deviation from baseline warrants assessment of possible medication effects and other causes before treating it as usual low initiation.
takeaway: Assess a new change in alertness and function rather than treating it as baseline low initiation.
subtopic: New functional change during mental-health treatment
learningObjective: Assess a new change in alertness and function rather than treating it as baseline low initiation.

title: Coping with noncommand voices
stem: A client with distressing noncommand voices chooses quiet music during a simple craft task. Which follow-up finding best supports continuing this coping strategy?
options: The client keeps the music on throughout the session
Distress falls and the client resumes the chosen task
The client names several other available coping strategies
The client describes the music as familiar from childhood
why: Use alone does not show whether the strategy improves distress or functioning.
Improved comfort with resumed activity demonstrates a useful effect; continue reassessing symptoms and safety.
Knowledge of alternatives may help planning but does not evaluate the selected music strategy.
Familiarity may matter to preference but does not by itself establish clinical benefit.
takeaway: Evaluate individualized coping strategies for distressing hallucinations.
learningObjective: Evaluate individualized coping strategies for distressing hallucinations.
